questions.q: What question does a backtest actually answer?
options: Whether the strategy will be profitable in the future
What would have happened if this exact rule set ran over this historical window, under stated assumptions
Whether the strategy is legal to trade
What the strategy's maximum possible profit is
questions.explain: A backtest is a simulation of a specific rule set over a specific historical window under stated data and execution assumptions — not a forecast of future performance.

questions.q: A signal is computed from today's closing price. When is the earliest bar on which that signal can be traded without look-ahead bias?
options: Today's close, the same bar the signal was computed on
Today's open, before the close is known
The next bar after today's close (e.g. tomorrow's open)
It doesn't matter as long as the signal is correct
questions.explain: Today's closing price is only known after the market closes, so the earliest point a decision based on it can be acted on is the following bar.

questions.q: In the pandas pattern `signal.shift(1) * price.pct_change()`, what is the `.shift(1)` doing?
options: Smoothing the signal with a moving average
Delaying the signal by one bar so it can't be paired with the return it was computed from
Converting the signal from a boolean to an integer
Reversing the sign of the signal
questions.explain: Shifting the signal forward by one period ensures the position used to compute a given bar's return was known before that bar's return began accruing — avoiding look-ahead bias.

questions.q: Which of the five parts of a backtest's anatomy do naive, beginner backtests most commonly oversimplify?
options: Data and signal
Signal and position
Execution and P&L
Data and P&L
questions.explain: Naive backtests often get data, signal, and position right but assume instant, free, exact-price fills — oversimplifying execution, which then distorts the resulting P&L.

questions.q: Which of the following is something a backtest, by itself, CANNOT tell you?
options: What a rule's historical P&L would have been under the stated assumptions
How the equity curve was distributed over the test period
Whether the measured edge is real or an artifact of fitting to the same data being tested
How sensitive the result is to changing a parameter
questions.explain: Distinguishing a real edge from a statistical artifact of overfitting requires out-of-sample testing and further validation — a single backtest result cannot settle that question alone.
